name: Operational UX
contentMarkdown:
# Operational UX

Operational UX describes the design of interfaces and workflows that people use to carry out recurring business operations. It focuses on completing work accurately, understanding its status, and handling exceptions across roles and systems.

The term is used descriptively rather than as a single standardized method. Relevant products include reservation tools, support queues, inventory systems, and enterprise administration interfaces.

## Example: processing a booking queue

A travel operations team needs to identify bookings awaiting ticket issuance. A useful workspace could show the booking reference, departure date, owner, current status, and the reason a booking is blocked.

Opening a booking should preserve enough queue context for the operator to return to the right place. A handoff should identify the next owner and any unresolved work. If ticket issuance fails, the interface should distinguish a confirmed failure from an unknown outcome that needs checking before retrying.

These details affect the quality of the operation as much as the speed of an individual click.

## What to evaluate

Choose measures that reflect the actual workflow, such as successfully completed cases, handling time, rework, and handoff delays. Review them together: faster handling can conceal more downstream corrections.

Test common tasks alongside exceptions, interruptions, and permission changes. Pay particular attention to selection scope in bulk actions, unsaved work, and stale data.

Support keyboard operation and readable information density. When implementing an interactive data grid, provide its required focus management and keyboard behavior. A visual table does not automatically need the ARIA grid role.

Evaluate the complete task with operators, including the tools and information they use outside the product.

## Related terms

- [Enterprise Information Architecture](/glossary/enterprise-information-architecture.html)
- [State Transition Matrix](/glossary/state-transition-matrix.html)
- [Semantic Zoom](/glossary/semantic-zoom.html)
- [Interaction Invariant](/glossary/interaction-invariant.html)

name: Service Blueprinting
contentMarkdown:
# Service Blueprinting

Service blueprinting is a method for mapping how an organization delivers a service. A service blueprint connects customer actions with the visible interactions, backstage work, and supporting processes that make those interactions possible.

## What does a service blueprint include?

Start with a specific customer journey and map the service work around it. The line of interaction marks customer contact with the organization. The line of visibility separates work customers can see from work behind the scenes. The line of internal interaction separates customer-facing staff from supporting functions.

Include evidence such as forms, messages, and documents that participants encounter. Add owners, dependencies, and timing where they help explain how the service works.

## Example: Changing a flight

This simplified blueprint follows a traveler who wants to move a booked flight.

| Layer | Request the change | Review the option | Complete the change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Customer action | Asks for a Friday flight. | Reviews the price and terms. | Approves the change and pays any amount due. |
| Frontstage interaction | The app acknowledges the request. | An agent presents the quote and its expiry. | The app reports the outcome. |
| Backstage action | An agent checks the booking and fare rules. | The booking system calculates a new fare. | Ticketing issues the revised ticket after the required checks. |
| Supporting processes and systems | Maintain booking records and access to fare inventory. | Provide pricing and payment services. | Process payment where needed and deliver confirmation. |
| Evidence | Request acknowledgment. | Dated quote and change conditions. | Revised ticket and confirmation message. |

The map can reveal a gap between payment and ticket issuance. The team can identify who handles a failure at that point, what confirms successful issuance, and what the traveler should be told while the issue is resolved.

## How do you use a blueprint?

Walk through the actual service with frontline and operations staff, supported by customer research and operational records. Mark uncertain steps, assign owners to the most important gaps, and test the proposed changes. A journey map supplies the customer’s perspective. The blueprint adds the work and dependencies behind that experience.

## Related terms

- [Customer Journey Mapping](/glossary/customer-journey-mapping.html)
- [Operational UX](/glossary/operational-ux.html)
- [Information Architecture (IA)](/glossary/information-architecture.html)

## Sources

- [Service Blueprints: Definition, Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprints-definition/)
- [Service Blueprinting FAQ, Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/service-blueprinting-faq/)

name: Structural Navigation Model
contentMarkdown:
# Structural Navigation Model

A structural navigation model describes the main and local paths people use to move through a product's information architecture. It shows how sections and views are organized, what users can reach from each level, and how they can move back to a broader view.

## How does structural navigation differ from contextual navigation?

Structural navigation follows the product's organization. For example, **Trips → Trip details → Bookings** follows a section down to a local view. Contextual navigation connects related information where a user needs it. A link from a trip's traveler list to a Traveler record is a contextual route that can cross sections.

Keep a record’s name and identifying details consistent across entry points. An agent who arrives from search should recognize the same booking they see on a trip.

## Navigation example for a travel operations tool

| Route | Design decision |
|---|---|
| Main menu → Trips → Trip details | Trips gives agents a stable starting point for work organized around trips. |
| Trip details → Bookings | Local navigation keeps a trip's bookings within reach while the agent reviews that trip. |
| Trip details → Traveler record | A contextual link lets the agent inspect a related traveler and their other trips. |
| Search → Booking details | A direct entry should show the booking's identity and link to its trip when the user has access. |

The [object map](/glossary/object-mapping.html) explains which records are related. Use the navigation model to choose which relationships become routes. Use the product's hierarchy to choose the breadcrumb trail. Use a separate return control when agents need to get back to a filtered list.

## How do you design and test the model?

1. **Start with common tasks.** Identify where users begin and which views they need to reach. Choose main sections and local views that match those tasks.
2. **Add useful contextual links.** Decide which related records users need nearby. Use [cardinality](/glossary/cardinality-ux-architecture.html) to anticipate how many results a path may expose.
3. **Plan orientation and return paths.** Check that titles, local navigation, and breadcrumbs make sense on direct entry. For an agent returning from a booking, consider whether the trip's prior list filters should be restored.
4. **Test the routes separately.** Use tree testing to evaluate labels and hierarchy. Use a prototype to test contextual links and direct entry, where placement and screen context matter.

Test whether an agent can open a booking from search, find its trip, and return to the booking list without losing their place.

## Related terms

- [Information Architecture (IA)](/glossary/information-architecture.html)
- [Wayfinding System](/glossary/wayfinding-system.html)
- [Breadcrumb Hierarchy](/glossary/breadcrumb-hierarchy.html)
- [Polyhierarchy](/glossary/polyhierarchy.html)

## Sources

- [Designing Web Navigation: Types of Navigation Summary, James Kalbach](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/designing-web-navigation/9780596528102/ch04s03.html)
- [Object-Oriented UX, Sophia V. Prater](https://alistapart.com/article/object-oriented-ux/)
- [Tree Testing: Evaluate Menu Labels and Categories, Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tree-testing/)

name: State Transition Matrix
contentMarkdown:
# State Transition Matrix

A state transition matrix is a table that shows which events can trigger a transition from each state and what state follows. UX teams use it to design actions, feedback, and recovery paths for objects such as bookings, tickets, and purchase requests.

## How do you read a state transition matrix?

Rows show current states. Columns show events, which can come from a user or an external system. A cell identifies the next state for that combination. When a transition depends on a rule, record the condition, also called a guard.

## Example of a booking state transition matrix

In this example, an agent submits a booking and waits for the supplier to confirm it. Cancellation also requires a supplier response. While cancellation is pending, the agent can see the request status and cannot submit a second request.

| Current state | Submit booking | Confirm booking | Request cancellation | Accept cancellation | Decline cancellation |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Draft | Awaiting confirmation | — | — | — | — |
| Awaiting confirmation | — | Confirmed | — | — | — |
| Confirmed | — | — | Cancellation pending | — | — |
| Cancellation pending | — | — | — | Canceled | Confirmed |
| Canceled | — | — | — | — | — |

A dash means the event has no valid transition in this example. Confirming the booking and accepting or declining cancellation are supplier events. The booking moves out of Draft once a complete submission succeeds. An agent can request cancellation only when their role and the fare rules allow it. If the supplier declines cancellation, restore Confirmed status and show the reason if available.

This example covers the confirmation path and two cancellation outcomes. Extend the model for booking rejection, timeouts, and other cases your product supports.

## How does the matrix inform ORCA actions?

The Calls to Action part of [ORCA](/glossary/orca-framework.html) identifies actions people need. The matrix helps specify how those actions behave at each stage of the object's lifecycle. For example, agents can see “Cancellation pending” in the booking list and open the detail view to check when the request was sent.

Record what users see when an event fails or arrives late. If a booking changed after the agent opened it, refresh its status and explain why the requested action cannot proceed. Use the same rules in list and detail views.

Review the table with design, engineering, and operations. Walk through one routine case, one blocked action, and one delayed response. Add missing transitions or feedback before the workflow is built.

## Related terms

- [Object-Oriented UX](/glossary/object-oriented-ux.html)
- [ORCA Framework](/glossary/orca-framework.html)
- [Operational UX](/glossary/operational-ux.html)
- [Interaction Invariant](/glossary/interaction-invariant.html)

## Sources

- [State Chart XML (SCXML), W3C](https://www.w3.org/TR/scxml/)
- [Introducing ORCA, Sophia V. Prater](https://medium.com/design-bootcamp/introducing-orca-the-third-diamond-in-your-ux-process-23a1babb0389)

name: Polyhierarchy
contentMarkdown:
# Polyhierarchy

A polyhierarchy is a hierarchical classification structure in which a concept can have more than one immediate broader concept. It lets people reach the same concept through different valid category paths.

For example, “Design tokens” could appear under both “Design systems” and “Design engineering.” Both paths lead to the same glossary entry. The entry does not need to be copied to support multiple placements.

SKOS permits multiple broader relationships, making it one way to represent this structure.

## Polyhierarchy and faceted classification

Polyhierarchy organizes broader and narrower concepts. Faceted classification describes items through separate dimensions.

In a resource library, a guide might be placed under both “Accessibility” and “Design systems.” Its facets might separately describe format, reading level, and publication date.

These approaches can work together. The distinction helps teams decide whether an additional placement expresses a category relationship or whether the attribute belongs in a filter.

## Example: two routes to one resource

A component documentation page could be reachable through “Components → Form controls → Date picker” and “Patterns → Booking → Date picker.”

In this example, the product keeps a single documentation record and stable URL. It can show a breadcrumb appropriate to the selected navigation context, with a clear route back to the relevant section.

## What to check

Use labels people understand, document the reason for each placement, and test whether users can find the resource through expected paths.

Avoid cycles that make a concept its own ancestor. If category paths generate different URLs for the same content, handle canonicalization deliberately. Multiple navigation placements do not require multiple indexable copies of a page.

## Related terms

- [Information Architecture (IA)](/glossary/information-architecture.html)
- [Faceted Classification](/glossary/faceted-classification.html)
- [Core Model](/glossary/core-model.html)
- [Controlled Vocabulary](/glossary/controlled-vocabulary.html)

## Sources

- [W3C: SKOS Primer — Semantic Relationships](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-primer/)
- [W3C: SKOS Reference — Semantic Relations](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-reference/)
